facts: If AI means the current generation of tools rather than earlier machine learning, I started using AI for programming a little less than six months before the original interview. I see similarities between current AI and earlier machine learning, in which inputs are supplied to a model to receive assistance or answers.

At work in an enterprise company I am restricted to permitted AI tools. Privately I try to experiment with as many accessible and reasonably priced tools as possible so I can be prepared for rapid changes in AI.

Until roughly six months before the original interview I had paid little attention to AI developments, much as I had paid little attention to earlier machine learning. Seeing improvements in spelling and translation tools, I tested AI on coding or work tasks and was surprised by its capabilities. That motivated me to learn more for job security and preparedness. I use GitHub Copilot but have not used Cursor; I know developers who started with Cursor and later moved to other tools.

I do not feel I need a separate AI-oriented IDE because VS Code already meets my needs, although I have not tried Cursor. I have used ChatGPT and only recently started experimenting with Claude, prompted by reports of its client source-code leak.

At the original interview I described reports that nearly half a million lines of the Claude Code client's source code had been exposed roughly ten to twelve days earlier. I believed developers had rewritten the client in Python and TypeScript within the preceding five to ten days, to comply with licensing constraints and allow alternative model providers. These were my contemporaneous claims, not independently verified facts.

I believed a rewritten Claude Code client allowing alternative models had attracted about 180,000 GitHub stars in a few days. I was interested in experimenting without what I understood to be a $100–200 monthly subscription and possible additional token costs. I also believed Anthropic was trying to restrict third-party API access and remove repositories, possibly pursuing legal action. I described the situation as rapidly changing and unprecedented in my experience; these were my beliefs and es

Reports of a large AI provider accidentally exposing its own code made me question whether our company [COMPANY] should allow AI to scan our core software. I speculated that the leak could have resulted from human error or automation exposing architecture and decisions; I did not know the actual cause.
I also use Gemini and mentioned a tool called Kilo (K-I-L-O) in my survey. I noted that many AI tools were appearing.
Some of the AI tools I use are integrated directly into my IDE.
I use IDE-integrated AI sometimes, not always.

I have safety concerns about IDE-integrated AI potentially acting beyond what I intend. I need to understand its permissions and restrictions before allowing it access to a folder or drive. Sometimes I prefer chat because it exposes only the source code I paste or attach.
Safety is the reason I sometimes prefer AI chat to unrestricted IDE integration.
It is tempting and exciting to let AI autonomously find and optimize everything possible, but I have observed that this unrestricted approach produces varying results.
Because autonomous AI can produce inconsistent results, I am not particularly fond of letting it run unrestricted.

I am a very senior developer with few colleagues available for technical sparring. When revisiting a language or library after a long absence, I would prefer discussing its pros and cons with an experienced colleague rather than reading extensive documentation. My main AI use is as a sparring partner for ideas, concepts and inspiration about implementation and logic.

I currently use AI rarely for debugging because I tend to debug my own code myself. If AI initially produced the code, I might ask it to continually fix errors and thus use AI debugging much more in future. I sometimes use AI to understand unfamiliar code without going deeply into details. I began discussing a company group testing Claude for refactoring.

A colleague leading our Claude testing group is trying to refactor a whole application for Linux compatibility rather than Windows only, allowing Claude considerable freedom; I do not yet know the outcome. Personally I almost never or never use AI for refactoring, never use it for writing tests, and write tests myself only when they make sense rather than merely satisfying management checkboxes. I referred jokingly to the saying about real developers working only in production. I almost never us
I use AI often for explaining concepts and learning, which is among my main uses. I also use AI often for writing and generating code, since generating code is the direct output when I request it.

One or two weeks before Easter, I investigated a longstanding technical problem one evening after work. I had several alternative tools (roughly eight to ten, as transcribed) for pre- and post-processing but had not explored this particular concept. The original documentation concerned C# and a binary payload to the frontend; I am not primarily a C# developer. I used Copilot Chat with only the documentation to isolate understanding of the binary stream instead of giving it the whole project. I a
For the binary-stream visualization task I specifically used Copilot Chat.

A few days before the interview I also experimented with Claude, but do not yet feel skilled at orchestrating it to avoid random guesses or poor decisions. I am exploring skills, MCP and providing a documentation base, for example a React skill or designated documentation instead of arbitrary web searches.

In my experience AI sometimes uses documentation for the wrong library version even when I explicitly specify the map library version and a React version such as 19, causing errors in the generated implementation.

I have repeatedly instructed AI to use an exact dependency version without improvising, yet it still used something else until I showed a screenshot of the package configuration. I think expensive models can do impressive work but also produce unused, duplicated or poor-quality code unless explicitly told to clean it up. Experienced developers need to recognize these issues, such as redundant variable names. I compare prompting to pulling a slot-machine lever and waiting to see the output.

I believe AI output depends on input quality and that better skills for specifying goals, decomposing logic and defining architecture could improve my results. I have not developed these skills much yet. A colleague leading our Claude group had shifted from coding to writing what I recall as about 6,000 lines of Markdown in 50 files, which I find unappealing because I enjoy solving programming puzzles. I rewrote frontend principles for [COMPANY] and imagine AI could turn those guidelines into nu

At work we are supposed to follow agile Scrum, decomposing epics into user stories and tasks, estimating and refining them. Often we use an Azure agile board, but skip good descriptions, images or estimates; a task may be just a broad headline such as implementing a back-office interface, sometimes with child tasks. I think we have not found an ideal process. In projects with a dedicated Scrum master, daily stand-ups and strict sprint monitoring, even for a 10–15-person team, the process felt ex
For substantial real projects of over 1,000 hours, my workplace handles tasks more formally through agile and Scrum.
In my general working day I write code very often and review code almost never.

At [COMPANY] there was a proposal that developers regularly review one another's code to become involved and gain knowledge of each other's work. I began explaining that the usefulness depends in part on the programming language.

I am conservative about code review. I regard C++ and C# as more stable and constrained than JavaScript, where many problematic approaches still work. When asked about cross-frontend code review at [COMPANY], I argued that meaningful review requires understanding what the code does and its broader context, not simply looking at pull-request diffs. Otherwise comments may concern naming, camel case or loop style without improving the work and consume developers' time. Particularly in JavaScript I
I consider debugging and bug fixing part of normal coding, because implementing code, including my own, can introduce bugs elsewhere that I immediately fix.
Counting bugs fixed during ordinary implementation, I revised my general debugging and bug-fixing frequency to possibly very often.
I rated ordinary testing, running tests and smoke testing as almost never in my general work.
The kinds of testing I do are stress testing, integration testing and performance testing.
I agreed that stress, integration and performance testing occur more often than the ordinary testing I had rated almost never; the final words of this turn are unclear in the transcript.

I prioritize stability and performance testing, including speed, network traffic and latency. For example, I sometimes inadvertently choose a US cloud data center, producing high network latency that needs investigation. These issues matter more to me than a simple input-field test distinguishing numbers from text.
Of my frequently performed development activities, writing code takes the most of my time.

For at least the four years before the interview I have often had to fix other people's code, which I find difficult and dislike. In React, tangled code can work despite poor structure; even highly structured unidirectional data-flow code with display components receiving data can be hard to understand, and a quick fix may take longer than in tangled code. I often face both situations. I rely on persistence, trial and error, logging, breakpoints and runtime debugging to understand unfamiliar cod

If the author of unfamiliar code is still available, I would ask them to fix it or explain why it was written that way and whether another part of the system depends on that choice. But I estimate that in roughly nine out of ten cases the original author is not available.
When the original author is unavailable, I rely on debugging and trial and error to understand their code.
When working on code written by others, I try to understand as much of it as I can.

I used AI when writing frontend-community guidelines. I already knew the content and its pros, cons and approaches from years of experience, but find spelling, grammar and consistency of tense difficult because I am dyslexic. I wanted correct and polished English for native English readers, so I asked AI to check spelling and wording, suggest better phrasing and adjust the tone. My key message was that our science-sector company needs to keep testing cutting-edge frontend/browser technologies to

I have previously written documentation, principles and guides manually without AI, though not necessarily an enterprise rulebook. It took much longer because I had to check spelling and grammar while expressing my thoughts, and my tense and writing voice could vary as if several people wrote it.

I validate AI-polished text by reading it multiple times, checking that it sounds good, conveys my main point and maintains the intended emphasis. Since I authored the ideas and have relevant expertise I can assess the output; without that knowledge I would not be able to validate it in the same way.

I worry about a moral conflict between our company's green-energy and sustainability values and AI's energy consumption. I hope cleaner electricity or more efficient chips and models could help. A design colleague showed me roughly 80 prompt iterations to reposition a button, which I speculated could cost around $100 or more, rather than making a simple manual change. In my own work I notice reduced ownership, passion and willingness to read or fix AI-generated code; instead I reflexively prompt
I think the research should examine AI-induced laziness because I have noticed and dislike becoming lazier myself when using AI.
I acknowledged that AI may also offer benefits and leave room for people to undertake other work; the wording of this response is incomplete.
I referred to the possibility of using freed-up capacity for many tasks or difficult problems.

entries.text: 提示注入与模型幻觉应作概念区分：提示注入是不可信输入试图改变模型应遵守的任务或指令；模型幻觉是模型输出缺少可靠依据或包含错误断言的现象。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。
持续集成（continuous integration）：每次代码变更后自动执行构建与测试的流程。
测试集与过拟合应作概念区分：测试集是在模型开发完成后估计泛化表现的数据；过拟合是模型学习了训练样本特有噪声而难以泛化。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。

entries.topic: 无监督学习与强化学习
entries.text: 无监督学习与强化学习应作概念区分：无监督学习是从无标签数据中发现结构或模式；强化学习是通过环境反馈和奖励优化行动策略。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。
训练集与测试集应作概念区分：训练集是用于拟合模型参数的数据样本；测试集是在模型开发完成后估计泛化表现的数据。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。
测试集（test set）：在模型开发完成后估计泛化表现的数据。

entries.topic: 检索增强生成与代码审查
entries.text: 检索增强生成与代码审查应作概念区分：检索增强生成是生成前从外部资料检索相关证据并将其纳入上下文；代码审查是通过检查代码变更识别缺陷风险和可维护性问题。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。
单元测试与监督学习应作概念区分：单元测试是验证单个程序单元在指定条件下行为的测试；监督学习是用带标签样本拟合输入到输出的映射。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。
代码审查与模型幻觉应作概念区分：代码审查是通过检查代码变更识别缺陷风险和可维护性问题；模型幻觉是模型输出缺少可靠依据或包含错误断言的现象。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。
无监督学习与测试集应作概念区分：无监督学习是从无标签数据中发现结构或模式；测试集是在模型开发完成后估计泛化表现的数据。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。

entries.text: 大语言模型与提示注入应作概念区分：大语言模型是从大规模文本等序列学习条件生成分布的模型；提示注入是不可信输入试图改变模型应遵守的任务或指令。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。

训练集与数据泄漏应作概念区分：训练集是用于拟合模型参数的数据样本；数据泄漏是训练阶段不当使用了本应独立评估的信息。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。
